paras: The lynching of Wilson Arnold was the killing of a Black man, also named in the papers as Wilkes or Wilks Arnold, who was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Mississippi, by an armed mob on November 19, 1888, and hanged. Arnold had surrendered to the sheriff about a week earlier after shooting Captain Robert Johnson, a white planter, near Satartia, a killing he said was in self-defense. A Yazoo County grand jury later reported that it could not identify any of the lynchers, although about fifteen were said to be known.

According to a Yazoo City special to the New Orleans Picayune, Arnold, described as "colored," had surrendered saying he shot Johnson at Johnson's home near Satartia in self-defense. The Picayune called Johnson "one of the most prominent citizens of the county"; some papers placed the killing at Lake George.

The Savannah Morning News printed a different account of the killing, said to have been given by Arnold's wife and other witnesses to a citizens' meeting near the scene. In that telling, Arnold threw Johnson, who was "under the influence of liquor," to the ground, shot him in the temple and beat his head with an unloaded gun.

On the morning of November 19, a large number of Johnson's friends went to the jail and took Arnold, saying they meant to avenge the death of their friend and neighbor. The Times-Democrat's Yazoo City correspondent put the time at about 7 o'clock and described "an armed body of determined men" who carried Arnold back to the scene of the killing. A Memphis dispatch in the New York Evening World described instead a "cavalcade" of about seventy-five mounted men who surrounded the jail and demanded the prisoner.

By that account, Arnold had first been hidden away, but the jailer, thinking the trouble over, returned him to the jail. Soon afterward the lynchers took him a short distance from town and hanged him. Later items stated that he had been lynched or "hung by a mob," and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star put the mob at about one hundred men, "white and colored."

The only follow-up in the coverage came in December, when the Brookhaven Leader reported that the Yazoo County grand jury had been unable to discover any of the persons who lynched Arnold, although about fifteen men among the lynchers were known. In its report the jury stated its members' belief that several of the lynchers had appeared before them as witnesses.

The Picayune's Yazoo City special ran on November 20 in papers from Sacramento and Salt Lake City to Wilmington, Delaware, and later in the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner. Headlines treated Arnold's guilt as settled: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran "HE SWINGS" over "A Negro Murderer Lynched by Whites in Mississippi," and the Wilmington Evening Journal titled the dispatch "A Brutal Murder Revenged." The Savannah Morning News headlined its version "LYNCHING A NEGRO" and wrote that Arnold had probably "paid the debt for his fearful crime."

Northern weeklies reduced the case to a line in their news summaries, the Chicago Citizen and the Worthington Advance stating that Arnold was taken from jail on Monday and lynched "for the murder of Captain Robert Johnson." In Mississippi, the Grenada Sentinel and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star called Arnold "the slayer" and "the negro who brutally murdered" Johnson, and the Brookhaven Leader carried the grand jury report.

Arnold's self-defense claim conflicts with the version credited to witnesses at a citizens' meeting, which described an unprovoked killing; both reached print only through white papers. The papers also differed on who made up the mob, the Sacramento headline saying Arnold was lynched "by Whites" while the Savannah Morning News, the People and Patriot and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star said colored men joined the party.
The Grenada Sentinel dated the taking to "Sunday night," November 18, against the Monday morning given in the Yazoo City dispatches and most other papers.
